questions.question: Explain how mining has created settlements in South Africa, with three examples.
questions.expected_answer: When valuable minerals are found, people come to work in the mines, and shops, houses, schools, roads and railways follow. Kimberley grew after diamonds were found, especially on the hill that became the Big Hole in 1871. Johannesburg grew very fast after gold was found on the Witwatersrand in 1886. eMalahleni grew with coal, Rustenburg with platinum and Kathu with iron ore. When mines close, towns can shrink, like Pilgrim's Rest, which now depends on tourism.

questions.question: Explain how fishing and trade have influenced the location of settlements.
questions.expected_answer: The cold Benguela Current brings nutrient-rich water full of fish to the west coast, so fishing towns such as Lambert's Bay, St Helena Bay, Saldanha and Port Nolloth grew there with harbours and fish factories. Trade created ports such as Durban, Cape Town and Gqeberha where ships load and unload, railway junction towns such as De Aar, border towns such as Musina near Beitbridge, and market towns in farming areas.

questions.question: Describe how laws in the past and present have affected where people live in South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: The Natives Land Act of 1913 allowed black South Africans to own land only in small reserves, later homelands, far from jobs, so many men became migrant workers. The Group Areas Act of 1950 created separate areas for different race groups, and people were forcibly removed from places such as Sophiatown and District Six to townships on the edges of cities. Since 1994, these laws are gone: people may live anywhere, land restitution allows some to reclaim land, and planning laws guide where homes and factories are built.
